title: No. 22 Drifter Review: Uncompromised Speed – Miguel Ovalles
content:
After about 5,000 miles aboard No. 22 Bicycle Co‘s Drifter titanium gravel bike, including Unbound XL and a 4th place finish at Gravel Worlds 300, Miguel has penned a review of this dream machine. Read on for his words and some golden autumnal photos from the Southern Rockies by John below…

At the core of my Race Metal series, the goal has always been pretty simple: find the fastest metal bikes on the market.

I’m looking for bikes that show little to no disadvantage compared to modern carbon race bikes. But let’s face it: when it comes to pure racing, speed, and lightness, carbon is really hard to compete with. Carbon frames are getting lighter and more aerodynamic every year, and metal bikes can sometimes feel like they’ve been relegated to the adventure-focused rider who cares more about durability than outright speed.

Well, I refuse to fit in that box, and No. 22 seems to agree with me.

No. 22 Drifter Quick Hits

  • Frameset: $6,499
  • Super lightweight frame: ~3.5 lbs for the 58cm reviewed here
  • Bike weight: 20.5 lbs with bottle cages and computer mount
  • Seamless integrated cable routing
  • In-house stem and seatpost that match the frame perfectly
  • Beautiful 3D-printed dropouts and seatstays
  • 56 mm tire clearance
  • Super responsive and stiff in the right areas
  • Titanium construction that should last for decades

Putting aside the numbers and the features, the real test was going to be whether the Drifter could actually race, and I gave it a series of pretty serious tests.

Show Bikes Are Just Bikes

The bike came to me straight from Sea Otter. It was a show bike, spec’d like one: top-of-the-line components, a stylish finish, and details everywhere you looked. This Drifter looked almost too pretty to ride hard; John and Spencer even called it a Lambo.

But even show bikes are just bicycles, and I couldn’t wait to get some miles on it. My plan was to take the Drifter to Unbound XL, Gravel Worlds 300, and Mega Mid South. Three ultra races in the 300-mile range.

I was a little scared of damaging it, but the folks at No. 22 assured me they wanted me to race it hard. So I did.

No. 22 Bicycle Company

Bryce and Mike, the founders of No. 22, fell in love with one riding material: titanium. So much so that they named their company after it, the element with atomic number 22 on the periodic table.

They pay close attention to the ordering process, knowing that buying a custom bike can be a daunting experience for everyone involved. They also offer an impressive level of customization when it comes to finishes, with options ranging from anodizing and high polish to Cerakote.

If you want to read more about No. 22’s story and evolution, take a look at John’s 2023 review of the Drifter Adventure. Entitled “Lightfooted and Fancy”, John’s review period with that bike really helped him get back into riding shape by using it on one of our favorite loops here in Santa Fe. In fact, he shot the golden-hued photos you see here on the same loop.

Who Is the No. 22 Drifter For?

My first thought about bikes of this caliber and price was that they’re either a retirement gift for a cyclist or something a young person saves up for because they value a proper “forever bike.” Sure, not everyone can afford a bike with this level of craftsmanship, but then again, there are countless other options out there. It’s easy to say this is a doctor and dentist bike, yet you’ll see young people riding No. 22’s creations.

Perhaps someone lives somewhere without a car, so they save a lot of money each year that way. I’ve had deeper conversations with John about premium bikes, and his take was along the lines of: regardless of how premium they feel, they’re still cheaper than a car. In some cities, you can take public transit. For people who can make a bike their main mode of transportation, it can be an awesome, incredibly beautiful purchase that makes them cherish each and every ride.

As for the doctors and dentists: some folks make good money and want something flashy that stands out from the bikes in their riding circle. Nothing wrong with that either.

Those initial impressions I had have changed too. Let’s be honest here: premium carbon bikes from big brands can cost even more than the Drifter, which makes my head hurt when I see someone spending this kind of money on a production plastic bike that will ultimately end up in a landfill one day. Do you really need the same bike Keegan Swenson is riding? No. Would you be better served by a custom titanium bike made in the US by people who are pushing the limits of the material? For me, and for many readers of The Radavist, absolutely.

My goal with Race Metal remains the same: convince more people that they don’t need the same bike a pro rider is using, and that metal bikes can be incredibly fast while offering things carbon simply can’t. And when you buy from a small company based in the US, you’re supporting the people actually building these bikes.

Level 99 Titanium Wizards

There are many things to consider about titanium bikes. This is an ongoing conversation I love having with John over coffee: not all titanium bikes are created equal. It comes down to the quality of the tubing, how much shaping and butting goes into those tubes, and how the frame is designed around the material.

Some companies take it a step further by designing and manufacturing their own components to create a more complete package. At the echelon level, you start seeing 3D-printed and CNC-machined parts being used to tune the ride quality and create a unique look. No. 22 does all of this, which, in my humble opinion, makes them Level 99 titanium wizards.

There aren’t many of those in the world, and even fewer in the US. Others doing similar levels of wizardry are Sturdy, Firefly, Avalanche, and Prova, to name just a few. Obviously, all that attention to detail and the effort that goes into creating this kind of complete package comes at a premium price.

Ok, onto the Drifter itself.

No. 22 Drifter: Two Things I Immediately Noticed

1. Chainstay length

The geometry is custom for me, but it also matches their 58 cm offering almost to a T. That being said, the chainstay length on my Drifter is 443 mm. I was under the impression, or maybe I was just led to believe, that shorter chainstays were one of the ingredients needed to create the quick acceleration and snappiness a race bike should have.

I’ll admit, I didn’t even look at this number until weeks after receiving the bike. By then, I had already put a good amount of time into it, and my first rides were mesmerizing. The Drifter felt quicker and lighter than any other bike I had ridden. It wanted to catch air at every opportunity. Every little water bar, it wanted to get aloft. It was happy, playful, and incredibly fast to maneuver. So when I eventually looked at the geometry numbers, I was a little puzzled.

I asked Bryce and Mike, the founders of No. 22, about my observations. Their answer was that the overall package of the bike compensates for the slightly longer chainstays. Talking with John about it, he made another point that stuck with me: bigger bikes should generally have longer chainstays.

There isn’t one “perfect” chainstay length, and every size of a bike doesn’t need to be held to the 430mm standard I had somehow decided was the truth. As a rider’s saddle height increases, they get closer to the rear hub, which makes the bike’s front end want to lift more. This was something I hadn’t considered.

Fair enough, and after thousands of miles, I can say that whatever No. 22 is doing here, it’s working.

2. The Tubing Shapes

The downtube was another thing that fascinated me.

No. 22, like many builders, including guys like Tom Ritchey, achieved desired frame stiffness by shaping the downtube. Downtubes are where a lot of a bicycle’s torsion occurs. So to give the Drifter its desired ride quality, No. 22 flattened the downtube at the head tube vertically and then flattened it horizontally as it meets the bottom bracket. They also flattened the top tube horizontally at the head tube and vertically at the seat tube, locking the desired frame feel in with these profiles.

On top of the tubing specs and butting profile, I think this is where the Drifter gets much of its snap and power transfer. No. 22 uses different butting and tubing specs per size, and on custom geometry bikes, they can ensure the rider’s weight is being considered, too. The bike is stiff in the right areas, and you can definitely feel it when sprinting or riding out of the saddle. Put the power down, and the Drifter responds immediately.

The More You Look

No. 22’s Drifter has an abundance of beautiful details. The more I looked, the more I appreciated the attention the New York-based company put into it. The 3D-printed dropouts blend continuously into the chainstays and seatstays, and the 3D-printed chainstay yoke helps create the bike’s generous tire clearance while still allowing room for a 46-tooth chainring.

Then there’s all the titanium: the headset, spacers, stem, seatpost, seat collar, and cranks all match the bike like a dream. There are so many little details in this frame that you could stare at it forever. That’s part of what makes the Drifter interesting to me. You can tell No. 22 designed the bike as a whole package, not just a titanium frame with expensive parts bolted onto it.

The No. 6 Composites Gravel Fork

One of the few non-metal parts of this build is the gravel fork from No. 6 Composites, created by the same folks at No. 22. And you probably guessed it: The number 6 on the periodic table represents Carbon. This is a true suspension-corrected fork measuring 430 mm axle-to-crown, so you can pair this bike with a 40 mm gravel fork like the RockShox Rudy or Fox 32 Taper-Cast and keep the same fit.  It comes spec’d with everything you would need: dynamo light routing, fender mounts, a whopping 63 mm tire clearance, semi-internal or fully internal cable routing, and 3-pack accessory mounts. What else could you ask for in a carbon fork?

Racing a Lambo

According to my Strava, I’ve put:

  • 4,383 miles
  • 264 hours
  • 243,193 feet of climbing

… into this bike during the review period.

That includes all the training and preparation for Unbound XL and Gravel Worlds 300, two of my season’s main races. Mega Mid South is coming up on October 17, so we’ll hit 5,000 miles in no time. That means I’ve had plenty of time to get to know the Drifter and race it.

Read here for an in-depth look into Miguel’s Unbound XL setup

Unbound XL

Unbound XL was a crazy adventure, to put it mildly.

The start was hot and fast. When you have athletes like Robin Gemperle, Rob Britton, and Maddy Nutt on the start line, you know you’re in for a hard day on the bike. Even though I was dropped from the front group early, I felt great and settled into a strong pace. I found a group to work with, and we started passing a lot of people through the middle of the race.

At nightfall, everything changed. Picking my lines and staying alert became incredibly important. The grasslands of Kansas have some deep and sharp gravel, and when you’re riding in a group, rocks fly everywhere, smashing into wheels, bikes, and riders. That’s when having a strong titanium bike gave me a lot of confidence; I wasn’t worried about the integrity of the frame.

Around mile 165, it started raining cats and dogs. We rode straight into a legitimate storm, with lightning flashing in front of our group and no place to find shelter, or maybe we just couldn’t see it through the rain. Either way, our only choice was to keep pedaling. Eventually, the storm moved along, and our group of five or six riders dwindled down to three. Then came the mud. We hit our first muddy minimum-maintenance road, and that famous Kansas peanut butter lived up to its reputation.

I rode maybe ten feet before my entire bike was clogged and rendered completely unrideable. I spent the next ten minutes freeing the bike from the demon mud. Then the walking began… a good three to five miles of hike-a-bike through flooded grass that felt more like a swamp than a road.

Thankfully, all the water and rain eventually helped clean the bike enough for me to ride again. This was the other moment during the race when I was incredibly happy to be riding a metal bike. Everyone else was worried about destroying their bikes, as previous editions of this event had claimed hundreds of frames and drivetrains. Once we were through the mud, we were able to get back on the bikes and eventually made it to the gas station around mile 208. By then, our group was down to two riders, and thankfully we encountered a couple more at the gas station.

They lay down, defeated, while I went inside, got some water and food, and cleaned the mud off my shoes. By the time I was ready to get back on my bike, my companion had been talking to the other riders. They were dot-watching Robin Gemperle, who was at the front and tackling the next MMR section after our stop.

It had taken him about two hours to traverse a five-mile muddy section, which was enough to make these riders question whether they wanted to continue.

At first, I looked for other riders who might be ready to keep going (my first mistake). These are individual races. I shouldn’t need the company of other people or their approval to keep going. But I started listening more and more to what the other riders were saying and the doubt started creeping in. I began second-guessing everything.

Would I make it back in time before I had to leave for home? Was I putting myself at risk by continuing? Would I destroy the bike if I kept going? A bike that wasn’t even mine. That moment still haunts me. I didn’t quit because it got too hard; I quit before it got hard.

I was feeling strong, and I had everything I needed. The bike was running perfectly, and even though I knew I had a long hike ahead of me, I could have kept going. I learned a valuable lesson this race: Never quit when you’re off the bike. Keep pedaling a little further and see what happens. A flashback to my first ultra: Dark moments don’t last. I know all of these things, and I still called it quits and took the convenient Jeep back to the event.

Gravel Worlds 300

Going into Gravel Worlds 300, I had one big reassurance. After racing 208 miles at Unbound XL at a really high pace, I had zero pain or aches in my body.

I had recovered incredibly well and was ready to ride my bike again the next day, which surprised me and told me two things. My fitness was high, and my position on the bike was dialed. If you’ve ever had a bike that you feel like you know so well that you could ride thousands of miles without getting sore, you know how special and comforting that feeling is.

That’s exactly where I was with the Drifter. I was excited for Gravel Worlds 300 to be a real test of the bike, my setup, and my mindset. I was ready, and I was itching to do my best after not finishing Unbound XL. The race was fast and dry for the most part. We did get some rain and a little bit of mud, but even the MMRs were perfect. I ended up near the front of the race, toggling between third and fourth place for most of the 300 miles.

Playing mental and strategic games at the end of a long race isn’t really why I race, but there I was, battling for a podium place with another two riders. With 15 miles to go, we joined the 75-mile race, and its course, and a big group of about 20 riders came flying past us at 20 miles an hour. We quickly got onto their wheels, and that’s when I started seeing cross-eyed.

I felt myself getting dropped a couple of times, but a text from my coach kept resonating in my head:

“Give it everything.”

I managed to stay on the wheels, although I was too far back. The second-place rider got away from the group with a couple of miles to go, and Oty moved three or four wheels ahead of me as we entered a little section of singletrack before the finish. I pushed with everything I had and even sprinted at the finish line, by myself. Somewhere in those last miles, I remembered why I do this. These races are for me and my family. They’re a way to endure and overcome obstacles. I chase that feeling of not quitting, of keeping pedaling and pushing through the dark moments.

Back to the Bike

Going back into review mode, after thousands of miles of training and two long, hard races, the No. 22 Drifter has become one with me.

I was sore at the end of Gravel Worlds, but nothing in my body was signaling pain or discomfort. Even though this bike is incredibly quick and stiff, it also provides a level of comfort that I associate with the best flexy metal bikes. It doesn’t feel like I’m choosing between speed and comfort, which is probably the biggest compliment I can give it.

An Aside: A Pursuit of Uncompromised Speed

There are certain things I look for when choosing a bike I want to race for 300 miles. Geometry numbers and frame specs that I know work for me. Tire clearance, frame stiffness, weight, and, perhaps most importantly, how the bike handles when it’s loaded up for an ultra. There’s one compromise I’ve always assumed metal bikes have to make: aerodynamics.

Metal bikes aren’t exactly known for being aerodynamic. Skinny tubes and round shapes aren’t ideal when you start thinking about the turbulence created when air hits the headtube. That’s where carbon has a clear advantage. Carbon frames can be shaped in almost any way imaginable, creating larger, more aerodynamic profiles exactly where they’re needed without necessarily adding a ton of weight.

The Drifter has larger tubes than a traditional skinny-tubed steel bike, but it isn’t particularly aerodynamic. That’s where No. 22 has me really excited about what’s coming next. In 2024, No. 22 gave us our first glimpse of the Reactor Aero, an aero road bike designed from the ground up to compete with the fastest aero bikes on the market. The final production version has been refined over the last two years and was shown at the Made Bike Show this past summer.

Weighing in at 16.99 pounds, it’s insane. And even though the bike looks beefier than No. 22’s other offerings, their 3D-printing capabilities allow them to create the volume they need while keeping the weight under control. Orders for the Reactor Aero should start shipping by the end of the year. And if a gravel version of the Reactor Aero ever makes it into the wild…well, that might be the solution to all my problems (and the demise of all my savings).

TL;DR: Close to Perfection

I’m guilty of skipping through reviews and going straight to the part where all my questions will be answered in a few sentences. Don’t be like me; please read the whole thing. But just in case, here’s my attempt at summarizing the bike and my experience with it.

The No. 22 Drifter is fast, ridiculously light, and a rolling spectacle that you could look at for hours. The level of material selection and the different manufacturing methods No. 22 uses to turn the frame into a complete package, including matching titanium stems, seatposts, and headsets, puts them in a different league of titanium craftsmanship.

Its ride quality is unlike anything I’ve experienced on a titanium bike so far. The Drifter accelerates quickly, loves to catch air at every opportunity, and is incredibly fun to maneuver. At the same time, it’s a sure-footed bike capable of descending rough doubletrack, occasional singletrack, and even the arroyos around Santa Fe.

Almost 5,000 miles in, I don’t feel like I was riding a beautiful show bike anymore. I felt like I was riding my bike.

If your wallet can handle the price, or you’re considering a top-of-the-line carbon bike that would cost the same or potentially even more, I think No. 22 deserves your attention. You’re getting a beautifully crafted titanium bike built by a US company that is pushing what can be done with the material.

And after thousands of miles and two 200-plus-mile races, I can say this:

The Drifter doesn’t feel like a compromise. It just feels fast.

Pros

  • Lightweight
  • Made in the USA
  • 56 mm or 2.2” tire clearance
  • Beautiful Ti components
  • Integrated cable routing
  • 3D-printed chainstay yoke allows for a 46-tooth chainring
  • Feels like you’re racing a Lambo
  • Suspension-corrected fork

Cons

  • Expensive, but for what you’re getting, it’s worth it to the right customer
